entries.b1031cca7a18056e445ce0dfe22cf0c1babca8ee: <div sID="gen15849" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Isa.17" sID="Isa.17"/> <div eID="gen15849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15850" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15851" type="x-p"/> Syria and Ephraim were confederate against Judah (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.1-Isa.7.2">ch. vii. 1, 2</reference>), and, they being so closely linked together in their counsels, this chapter, though it be entitled "the burden of Damascus" (which was the head city of Syria), reads the doom of Israel too. I. The destruction of the strong cities both of Syria and Israel is here foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1-Isa.17.5">ver. 1-5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9-Isa.17.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. II. In the midst of judgment mercy is remembered to Israel, and a gracious promise made that a remnant should be preserved from the calamities and should get good by them, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6-Isa.17.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. III. The overthrow of the Assyrian army before Jerusalem is pointed at, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. In order of time this chapter should be placed next after <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.25">ch. ix.</reference>, for the destruction of Damascus, here foretold, happened in the reign of Ahaz, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2 Kings xvi. 9</reference>.
entries.82f0ec45d8f9dc18d1207584867bfbf2886fa56e: <div eID="gen15851" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15850" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Syria and Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 712.)</title> <div sID="gen15852" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus is taken away from <hi type="italic">being</hi> a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap. <hi type="super">2</hi> The cities of Aroer <hi type="italic">are</hi> forsaken: they shall be for flocks, which shall lie down, and none shall make <hi type="italic">them</hi> afraid. <hi type="super">3</hi> The fortress also shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria: they shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">4</hi> And in that day it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the glory of Jacob shall be made thin, and the fatness of his flesh shall wax lean. <hi type="super">5</hi> And it shall be as when the harvestman gathereth the corn, and reapeth the ears with his arm; and it shall be as he that gathereth ears in the valley of Rephaim. <div eID="gen15852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15853" type="x-p"/> We have here the burden of Damascus; the Chaldee paraphrase reads it, <hi type="italic">The burden of the cup of the curse to drink to Damascus in;</hi> and, the ten tribes being in alliance, they must expect to pledge Damascus in this cup of trembling that is to go round. 1. Damascus itself, the head city of Syria, must be destroyed; the houses, it is likely, will be burnt, as least the walls, and gates, and fortifications demolished, and the inhabitants carried away captive, so that for the present it is <hi type="italic">taken away from being a city,</hi> and is reduced not only to a village, but to <hi type="italic">a ruinous heap,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">v. 1</reference>. Such desolating work as this does sin make with cities. 2. The country towns are abandoned by their inhabitants, frightened or forced away by the invaders: <hi type="italic">The cities of Aroer</hi> (a province of Syria so called) <hi type="italic">are forsaken</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.2">v. 2</reference>); the conquered dare not dwell in them, and the conquerors have no occasion for them, nor did they seize them for want, but wantonness; so that the places which should be for men to live in are for <hi type="italic">flocks to lie down in,</hi> which they may do, and none will disturb nor dislodge them. Stately houses are converted into sheep-cotes. It is strange that great conquerors should pride themselves in being common enemies to mankind. But, how unrighteous soever they are, God is righteous in causing those cities to spue out their inhabitants, who by their wickedness had made themselves vile; it is better that <hi type="italic">flocks should lie down there</hi> than that they should harbour such as are in open rebellion against God and virtue. 3. The strongholds of Israel, the kingdom of the ten tribes, will be brought to ruin: <hi type="italic">The fortress shall cease from Ephraim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.3">v. 3</reference>), that in Samaria, and all the rest. They had joined with Syria in invading Judah very unnaturally; and now those that had been partakers in sin should be made partakers in ruin, and justly. When <hi type="italic">the fortress shall cease from Ephraim,</hi> by which Israel will be weakened, the kingdom will cease from Damascus, by which Syria will be ruined. The Syrians were the ring-leaders in that confederacy against Judah, and therefore they are punished first and sorest; and, because they boasted of their alliance with Israel, now that Israel is weakened they are upbraided with those boasts: "<hi type="italic">The remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel;</hi> those few that remain of the Syrians shall be in as mean and despicable a condition as the children of Israel are, and the glory of Israel shall be no relief or reputation to them." Sinful confederacies will be no strength, no stay, to the confederates, when God's judgments come upon them. See here what the glory of Jacob is when God contends with him, and what little reason Syria will have to be proud of resembling the glory of Jacob. (1.) It is wasted like a man in a consumption, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">The glory of Jacob</hi> was their numbers, that they were as the sand of the sea for multitude; but this glory <hi type="italic">shall be made thin,</hi> when many are cut off, and few left. Then the <hi type="italic">fatness of their flesh,</hi> which was their pride and security, <hi type="italic">shall wax lean,</hi> and the body of the people shall become a perfect skeleton, nothing but skin and bones. Israel died of a lingering disease; the kingdom of the ten tribes wasted gradually; God was to them <hi type="italic">as a moth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.5.12">Hos. v. 12</reference>. Such is all the glory of this world: it soon withers, and is made thin; but thee is a far more exceeding and external weight of glory designed for the spiritual seed of Jacob, which is not subject to any such decay—fatness of God's house, which will not <hi type="italic">wax lean.</hi> (2.) It is all gathered and carried away by the Assyrian army, as the corn is carried out of the field by the husbandmen, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.5">v. 5</reference>. The corn is the glory of the fields (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.13">Ps. lxv. 13</reference>); but, when it is reaped and gone, where is the glory? The people had by their sins made themselves ripe for ruin, and their glory was as quickly, as easily, as justly, and as irresistibly, cut down and taken away, as the corn is out of the field by the husbandman. God's judgments are compared to the <hi type="italic">thrusting in of the sickle when the harvest is ripe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Rev. xiv. 15</reference>. And the victorious army, like the careful husbandmen in the valley of Rephaim, where the corn was extraordinary, would not, if they could help it, leave an ear behind, would lose nothing that they could lay their hands on.
entries.0460604fbd46fdf548bc0bf58079730798324ac1: <div eID="gen15853" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Syria and Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 712.)</title> <div sID="gen15854" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two <hi type="italic">or</hi> three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four <hi type="italic">or</hi> five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> At that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect <hi type="italic">that</hi> which his fingers have made, either the groves, or the images. <div eID="gen15854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15855" type="x-p"/> Mercy is here reserved, in a parenthesis, in the midst of judgment, for a remnant that should escape the common ruin of the kingdom of the ten tribes. Though the Assyrians took all the care they could that none should slip out of their net, yet the meek of the earth were hidden in the day of the Lord's anger, and had their lives given them for a prey and made comfortable to them by their retirement to the land of Judah, where they had the liberty of God's courts. 1. They shall be but a small remnant, a very few, who shall be marked for preservation (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Gleaning grapes shall be left in it.</hi> The body of the people were carried into captivity, but here and there one was left behind, perhaps one of two in a bed when the other was taken, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.34">Luke xvii. 34</reference>. The most desolating judgments in this world are short of the last judgment, which shall be universal and which none shall escape. In times of the greatest calamity some are kept safe, as in times of the greatest degeneracy some are kept pure. But the fewness of those that escape supposes the captivity of the far greatest part; those that are left are but like the poor remains of an olive tree when it has been carefully shaken by the owner; if there be <hi type="italic">two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough</hi> (out of the reach of those that shook it), that is all. Such is the <hi type="italic">remnant according to the election of grace,</hi> very few in comparison with the multitudes that walk on in the broad way. 2. They shall be a sanctified remnant, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.7-Isa.17.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. These few that are preserved are such as, in the prospect of the judgment approaching, had repented of their sins and reformed their lives, and therefore were snatched thus as brands out of the burning, or such as having escaped, and becoming refugees in strange countries, were awakened, partly by a sense of the distinguishing mercy of their deliverance, and partly by the distresses they were still in, to return to God. (1.) They shall look up to their Creator, shall enquire, <hi type="italic">Where is God my Maker, who giveth songs in the night,</hi> in such a night of affliction as this? <reference osisRef="Job.35.10-Job.35.11">Job xxxv. 10, 11</reference>. They shall acknowledge his hand in all the events concerning them, merciful and afflictive, and shall submit to his hand. They shall give him the glory due to his name, and be suitably affected with his providences. They shall expect relief and succour from him and depend upon him to help them. Their <hi type="italic">eyes shall have respect</hi> to him, <hi type="italic">as the eyes of a servant to the hand of his master,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.132.2">Ps. cxxiii. 2</reference>. Observe, It is our duty at all times to have respect to God, to have our eyes ever towards him, both as our Maker (the author of our being and the God of nature) and as the Holy One of Israel, a God in covenant with us and the God of grace; particularly, when we are in affliction, our eyes must be towards the Lord, to <hi type="italic">pluck our feet out of the net</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Ps. xxv. 15</reference>); to bring us to this is the design of his providence as he is our Maker and the work of his grace as he is the Holy One of Israel. (2.) They shall look off from their idols, the creatures of their own fancy, shall no longer worship them, and seek to them, and expect relief from them. For God will be alone regarded, or he does not look upon himself as at all regarded. He that looks to his Maker must not <hi type="italic">look to the altars, the work of his hands,</hi> but disown them and cast them off, must not retain the least respect for <hi type="italic">that which his fingers have made,</hi> but break it to pieces, though it be his own workmanship—<hi type="italic">the groves and the images;</hi> the word signifies images made in honour of the sun and by which he was worshipped, the most ancient and most plausible idolatry, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deut. iv. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job xxxi. 26</reference>. We have reason to account those happy afflictions which part between us and our sins, and by sensible convictions of the vanity of the world, that great idol, cool our affections to it and lower our expectations from it.
entries.09091fb86b1a76a0b992b2fa2744a9f9d736cef7: <div eID="gen15855" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Syria and Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 712.)</title> <div sID="gen15856" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> In that day shall his strong cities be as a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch, which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation. <hi type="super">10</hi> Because thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation, and hast not been mindful of the rock of thy strength, therefore shalt thou plant pleasant plants, and shalt set it with strange slips: <hi type="super">11</hi> In the day shalt thou make thy plant to grow, and in the morning shalt thou make thy seed to flourish: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the harvest <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a heap in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow. <div eID="gen15856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15857" type="x-p"/> Here the prophet returns to foretel the woeful desolations that should be made in the land of Israel by the army of the Assyrians. 1. That the cities should be deserted. Even the strong cities, which should have protected the country, shall not be able to protect themselves: They <hi type="italic">shall be as a forsaken bough and an uppermost branch</hi> of an old tree, which has gone to decay, is forsaken of its leaves, and appears on the top of the tree, bare, and dry, and dead; so shall their strong cities look when the inhabitants have deserted them and the victorious army of the enemy pillaged and defaced them, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9">v. 9</reference>. They shall be as the cities (so it may be supplied) which the Canaanites left, the old inhabitants of the land, because of the children of Israel, when God brought them in with a high hand, to take possession of that good land, cities which they built not. As the Canaanites then fled before Israel, so Israel should now flee before the Assyrians. And herein the word of God was fulfilled, that, if they committed the same abominations, <hi type="italic">the land</hi> should <hi type="italic">spue them out, as it spued out the nations that were before them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">Lev. xviii. 28</reference>), and that as, while they had God on their side, <hi type="italic">one of them chased a thousand,</hi> so, when they had made him their enemy, <hi type="italic">a thousand</hi> of them should <hi type="italic">flee at the rebuke of one;</hi> so that in the cities should be desolation, according to the threatenings in the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.31">Lev. xxvi. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.51">Deut. xxviii. 51</reference>. 2. That the country should be laid waste, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.10-Isa.17.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Observe here, (1.) The sin that had provoked God to bring so great a destruction upon that pleasant land. It was <hi type="italic">for the iniquity of those that dwelt therein.</hi> "It is <hi type="italic">because thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation</hi> and all the great salvations he has wrought for thee, hast forgotten thy dependence upon him and obligations to him, and <hi type="italic">hast not been mindful of the rock of thy strength,</hi> not only who is himself a strong rock, but who has been thy strength many a time, or thou wouldst have been sunk and broken long since." Note, The God of our salvation is the rock of our strength; and our forgetfulness and unmindfulness of him are at the bottom of all sin. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> have we <hi type="italic">perverted our way, because we have forgotten the Lord our God,</hi> and so we undo ourselves. (2.) The destruction itself, aggravated by the great care they took to improve their land and to make it yet more pleasant. [1.] Look upon it at the time of the seedness, and it was all like a garden and a vineyard; that pleasant land was replenished with pleasant plants, the choicest of its own growth; nay, so nice and curious were the inhabitants that, not content with them, they sent to all the neighbouring countries for strange slips, the more valuable for being strange, uncommon, far-fetched, and dear-bought, though perhaps they had of their own not inferior to them. This was an instance of their pride and vanity, and (that ruining error) their affection to be <hi type="italic">like the nations. Wheat, and honey, and oil</hi> were their staple commodities (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Ezek. xxvii. 17</reference>); but, not content with these, they must have flowers and greens with strange names imported from other nations, and a great deal of care and pains must be taken by hot-beds to make these plants to grow; the soil must be forced, and they must be covered with glasses to shelter them, and early in the morning the gardeners must be up to make the seed to flourish, that it may excel those of their neighbours. The ornaments of nature are not to be altogether slighted, but it is a folly to be over-fond of them, and to bestow more time, and cost, and pains about them than they deserve, as many do. But here this instance seems to be put in general for their great industry in cultivating their ground, and their expectations from it accordingly; they doubt not but their plants will grow and flourish. But, [2.] Look upon the same ground at the time of harvest, and it is all like a wilderness, a dismal melancholy place, even to the spectators, much more to the owners; for <hi type="italic">the harvest shall be a heap,</hi> all in confusion, <hi type="italic">in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow.</hi> The harvest used to be a time of joy, of singing and shouting (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.10">ch. xvi. 10</reference>); but this harvest the hungry eat up (<reference osisRef="Job.5.5">Job v. 5</reference>), which makes it a day of grief, and the more because the plants were pleasant and costly (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.10">v. 10</reference>) and their expectations proportionably raised. The harvest had sometimes been a day of grief, if the crop was thin and the weather unseasonable; and yet in that case there was hope that the next would be better. But this shall be desperate sorrow, for they shall see not only this year's products carried off, but the property of the ground altered and their conquerors lords of it. The margin reads it, <hi type="italic">The harvest shall be removed</hi> (into the enemy's country or camp, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.33">Deut. xxviii. 33</reference>) <hi type="italic">in the day of inheritance</hi> (when thou thoughtest to inherit it), <hi type="italic">and there shall be deadly sorrow.</hi> This is a good reason why we should not lay up our treasure in those things which we may so quickly be despoiled of, but in that good part which shall never be taken away from us.
entries.70b80808637171bbd6d57e4d00d5f6f4eeced23f: <div eID="gen15857" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Syria and Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 712.)</title> <div sID="gen15858" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Woe to the multitude of many people, <hi type="italic">which</hi> make a noise like the noise of the seas; and to the rushing of nations, <hi type="italic">that</hi> make a rushing like the rushing of mighty waters! <hi type="super">13</hi> The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but <hi type="italic">God</hi> shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind. <hi type="super">14</hi> And behold at evening tide trouble; <hi type="italic">and</hi> before the morning he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not. This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us. <div eID="gen15858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15859" type="x-p"/> These verses read the doom of those that spoil and rob the people of God. If the Assyrians and Israelites invade and plunder Judah, if the Assyrian army take God's people captive and lay their country waste, let them know that ruin will be their lot and portion. They are here brought in, 1. Triumphing over the people of God. They relied upon their numbers. The Assyrian army was made up out of divers nations: it was <hi type="italic">the multitude of many people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">v. 12</reference>), by which weight they hoped to carry the cause. They were very noisy, like the roaring of the seas; they talked big, hectored, and threatened, to frighten God's people from resisting them, and all their allies from sending in to their aid. Sennacherib and Rabshakeh, in their speeches and letters, made a mighty noise to strike a terror upon Hezekiah and his people; the nations that followed them <hi type="italic">made a rushing like the rushing of many waters,</hi> and those mighty ones, that threaten to bear down all before them and carry away every thing that stands in their way. <hi type="italic">The floods have lifted up their voice, have lifted up their waves;</hi> such is the tumult of the people, and the heathen, when they rage, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Ps. ii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3">xciii. 3</reference>. 2. Triumphed over by the judgments of God. They thought to carry their point by dint of noise; but woe to them (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">v. 12</reference>), for he <hi type="italic">shall rebuke them,</hi> that is, God shall, one whom they little think of, have no regard to, stand in no awe of; he shall give them a check with an invisible hand, <hi type="italic">and</hi> then <hi type="italic">they shall flee afar off.</hi> Sennacherib, and Rabshakeh, and the remains of their forces, shall run away in a fright, and shall be chased by their own terrors, <hi type="italic">as the chaff of the mountains</hi> which stand bleak <hi type="italic">before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind,</hi> like thistle-down (so the margin); they make themselves <hi type="italic">as chaff before the wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.5">Ps. xxxv. 5</reference>) and then <hi type="italic">the angel of the Lord</hi> (as it follows there), the same angel that slew many of them, shall chase the rest. God will make <hi type="italic">them like a wheel,</hi> or rolling thing, and then <hi type="italic">persecute them with his tempest</hi> and <hi type="italic">make them afraid with his storm,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.83.13">Ps. lxxxiii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.15">15</reference>. Note, God can dispirit the enemies of his church when they are most courageous and confident, and dissipate them when they seem most closely consolidated. This shall be done suddenly (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">At evening-tide</hi> they are very troublesome, and threaten trouble to the people of God; but <hi type="italic">before the morning they are not.</hi> At sleeping time they are cast into a deep sleep, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.5-Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 5, 6</reference>. It was in the night that the angel routed the Assyrian army. God can in a moment break the power of his church's enemies, even when it appears most formidable; and this is written for the encouragement of the people of God in all ages, when they find themselves an unequal match for their enemies; for <hi type="italic">this is the portion of those that spoil us,</hi> they shall themselves be spoiled. God will plead his church's cause, and those that meddle do it to their own hurt.  <chapter eID="Isa.17"/> <div eID="gen15859" type="x-p"/>

entries.b02c97e2311cfcbfbd8b1a46c54e9827a219d38f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8624"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 17</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.17.1-Isa.17.11">Is 17:1-11</reference>. Prophecy Concerning Damascus and Its Ally Samaria, that is, Syria and Israel, which had leagued together (seventh and eighth chapters).</title> <div sID="gen14168" type="x-p"/> Already, Tiglath-pileser had carried away the people of Damascus to Kir, in the fourth year of Ahaz (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>); but now in Hezekiah's reign a further overthrow is foretold (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.23">Jr 49:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.1">Zec 9:1</reference>). Also, Shalmaneser carried away Israel from Samaria to Assyria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.10">18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.11">11</reference>) in the sixth year of Hezekiah of Judah (the ninth year of Hoshea of Israel). This prophecy was, doubtless, given previously in the first years of Hezekiah when the foreign nations came into nearer collision with Judah, owing to the threatening aspect of Assyria.<div eID="gen14168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8624"/><hi type="bold">1. Damascus--</hi>put before Israel (Ephraim, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.3">Is 17:3</reference>), which is chiefly referred to in what follows, because it was the prevailing power in the league; with it Ephraim either stood or fell (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.1-Isa.7.25">Is 7:1-25</reference>). <div eID="gen14169" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1f4c4a88a47ce495481062b66677f2f066cedee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8625"/><div sID="gen14170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8625"/><hi type="bold">2. cities of Aroer--</hi>that is, the cities round Aroer, and under its jurisdiction [Gesenius]. So "cities with their villages" (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference>); "Heshbon and all her cities" (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.17">Jos 13:17</reference>). Aroer was near Rabbahammon, at the river of Gad, an arm of the Jabbok (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.5">2Sa 24:5</reference>), founded by the Gadites (<reference osisRef="Num.32.34">Nu 32:34</reference>).<div eID="gen14170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for flocks--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.5.17">Is 5:17</reference>). <div eID="gen14171" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3ba1e39edac5f20dfa0a17f0cdf04fd3edb05d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8626"/><div sID="gen14172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8626"/><hi type="bold">3. fortress ... cease--</hi>The strongholds shall be pulled down (Samaria especially: <reference osisRef="Hos.10.14">Ho 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.6">Mi 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.10">Ha 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remnant of Syria--</hi>all that was left after the overthrow by Tiglath-pileser (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>).<div eID="gen14173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the glory of ... Israel--</hi>They shall meet with the same fate as Israel, their ally. <div eID="gen14174" type="x-p"/>
entries.afb91a84acfc1e544dac99cb27bba277d06066dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8627"/><div sID="gen14175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8627"/><hi type="bold">4. glory of Jacob--</hi>the kingdom of Ephraim and all that they rely on (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.2">Ho 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.5">Mi 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fatness ... lean--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Is 10:16</reference>). <div eID="gen14176" type="x-p"/>
entries.601ba255af15145836e2b5a0c49d8e926eca5925: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8628"/><div sID="gen14177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8628"/><hi type="bold">5. harvestman, &c.--</hi>The inhabitants and wealth of Israel shall be swept away, and but few left behind just as the husbandman gathers the corn and the fruit, and leaves only a few gleaning ears and grapes (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.9-2Kgs.18.11">2Ki 18:9-11</reference>).<div eID="gen14177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with his arm--</hi>He collects the standing grain with one arm, so that he can cut it with the sickle in the other hand.<div eID="gen14178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Rephaim--</hi>a fertile plain at the southwest of Jerusalem toward Beth-lehem and the country of the Philistines (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.18-2Sam.5.22">2Sa 5:18-22</reference>). <div eID="gen14179" type="x-p"/>
entries.edb99df9c276449eab65458735a57b98cdf56398: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8629"/><div sID="gen14180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8629"/><hi type="bold">6. in it--</hi>that is, in the land of Israel.<div eID="gen14180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">two or three ... in the top--</hi>A few poor inhabitants shall be left in Israel, like the two or three olive berries left on the topmost boughs, which it is not worth while taking the trouble to try to reach. <div eID="gen14181" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e40c6c90cacfcbc35c7ce9ac06b4833a7a811dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8630"/><div sID="gen14182" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8630"/><hi type="bold">7. look to his Maker--</hi>instead of trusting in their fortresses--(<reference osisRef="Isa.17.3">Is 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.7">Mi 7:7</reference>). <div eID="gen14182" type="x-p"/>
entries.b386ad0c863c6d54f2ee58c80906353c3f8893a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8631"/><div sID="gen14183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8631"/><hi type="bold">8. groves--</hi>A symbolical tree is often found in Assyrian inscriptions, representing the hosts of heaven ("Saba"), answering to Ashteroth or Astarte, the queen of heaven, as Baal or Bel is the king. Hence the expression, "image of the grove," is explained (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.7">2Ki 21:7</reference>).<div eID="gen14183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">images--</hi>literally, "images to the sun," that is, to Baal, who answers to the sun, as Astarte to the hosts of heaven (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Ki 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>). <div eID="gen14184" type="x-p"/>
entries.306f1e5471ea1950c2a7029d9ed2cccbf5b37a99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8632"/><div sID="gen14185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8632"/><hi type="bold">9. forsaken bough--</hi>rather "the leavings of woods," what the axeman leaves when he cuts down the grove (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Is 17:6</reference>).<div eID="gen14185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which they left because of--</hi>rather, "which (the enemies) shall leave for the children of Israel"; literally, "shall leave (in departing) from before the face of the children of Israel" [Maurer]. But a few cities out of many shall be left to Israel, by the purpose of God, executed by the Assyrian. <div eID="gen14186" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2237fa71c8ede398620c1aa6da00be9434b2bfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8633"/><div sID="gen14187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8633"/><hi type="bold">10. forgotten ... God of ... salvation ... rock--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen14187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plants--</hi>rather, "nursery grounds," "pleasure-grounds" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set in--</hi>rather, "set them," the pleasure-grounds.<div eID="gen14189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strange slips--</hi>cuttings of plants from far, and therefore valuable. <div eID="gen14190" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fb52de8fc72e035121e511f770e34d0982a563b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8634"/><div sID="gen14191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8634"/><hi type="bold">11. In the day ... thy plant--</hi>rather, "In the day of thy planting" [Horsley].<div eID="gen14191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shalt ... make ... grow--</hi>Maurer translates, "Thou didst fence it," namely, the pleasure-ground. The parallel clause, "Make ... flourish," favors English Version. As soon as thou plantest, it grows.<div eID="gen14192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the morning--</hi>that is, immediately after; so in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.14">Psa 90:14</reference>, the Hebrew, "in the morning," is translated "early."<div eID="gen14193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but ... shall be a heap--</hi>rather, "but (promising as was the prospect) the harvest is gone" [Horsley].<div eID="gen14194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... day of grief--</hi>rather, "in the day of (expected) possession" [Maurer]. "In the day of inundation" [Horsley].<div eID="gen14195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of desperate sorrow--</hi>rather, "And the sorrow shall be desperate or irremediable." In English Version "heap" and "sorrow" may be taken together by hendiadys. "The heap of the harvest shall be desperate sorrow" [Rosenmuller].<div eID="gen14196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14197" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.18.7">Is 17:12-18:7</reference>. Sudden Destruction of a Great Army in Judea (namely that of the Assyrian Sennacherib), AND Announcement of the Event to the Ethiopian Ambassadors.<div eID="gen14197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14198" type="x-p"/> The connection of this fragment with what precedes is: notwithstanding the calamities coming on Israel, the people of God shall not be utterly destroyed (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.12">Is 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">13</reference>); the Assyrian spoilers shall perish (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">Is 17:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen14198" type="x-p"/>
entries.38eb32c3a200af4ef900fc1e1bec331fb7e6f2e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8635"/><div sID="gen14199" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8635"/><hi type="bold">12. Woe ... multitude--</hi>rather, "Ho (Hark)! a noise of," &c. The prophet in vision perceives the vast and mixed Assyrian hosts (Hebrew, "many peoples," see on <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>): on the hills of Judah (so "mountains," <reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">Is 17:13</reference>): but at the "rebuke" of God, they shall "flee as chaff."<div eID="gen14199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the rushing ... that make--</hi>rather, "the roaring ... roareth" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.23">Jr 6:23</reference>). <div eID="gen14200" type="x-p"/>
entries.edf954d5131e7d858d55fd8d701bb0f74c2c7083: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8636"/><div sID="gen14201" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8636"/><hi type="bold">13. shall ... shall--</hi>rather, "God rebuketh (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>) them, and they flee--are chased"; the event is set before the eyes as actually present, not future.<div eID="gen14201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chaff of ... mountains--</hi>Threshing floors in the East are in the open air on elevated places, so as to catch the wind which separates the chaff from the wheat (<reference osisRef="Ps.88.13">Psa 88:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.3">Ho 13:3</reference>).<div eID="gen14202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rolling thing--</hi>anything that rolls: stubble. <div eID="gen14203" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb5de3b1e56f2fe7f9bea217e39da1b748099987: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8637"/><div sID="gen14204" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8637"/><hi type="bold">14. eventide ... before morning--</hi>fulfilled to the letter in the destruction "before morning" of the vast host that "at eveningtide" was such a terror ("trouble") to Judah; on the phrase see <reference osisRef="Ps.90.6">Psa 90:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">30:5</reference>.<div eID="gen14204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is not--</hi>namely, the enemy.<div eID="gen14205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14206" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">us--</hi>the Jews. A general declaration of the doom that awaits the foes of God's people (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.17">Is 54:17</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.17"/>

entries.202838d929df76a93ee522ad8579271fa3991efb: <div eID="gen27219" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27220" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27221" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27221" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27220" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27222" type="x-p"/> Judgments of God upon Damascus, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1-Isa.17.3">Isa 17:1-3</reference>; and upon Israel, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.4-Isa.17.6">Isa 17:4-6</reference>. Good effects of these judgments on the small remnant or gleaning that should escape them, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.7">Isa 17:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.8">Isa 17:8</reference>. The same judgments represented in other but stronger terms, and imputed to irreligion and neglect of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9-Isa.17.11">Isa 17:9-11</reference>. The remaining verses are a distinct prophecy, a beautiful detached piece, worked up with the greatest elegance, sublimity, and propriety; and forming a noble description of the formidable invasion and sudden overthrow of Sennacherib, exactly suitable to the event, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.14">Isa 17:12-14</reference>. <div eID="gen27222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27223" type="x-p"/> This prophecy by its title should relate only to Damascus; but it full as much concerns, and more largely treats of, the kingdom of Samaria and the Israelites, confederated with Damascus and the Syrians against the kingdom of Judah. It was delivered probably soon after the prophecies of the seventh and eighth chapters, in the beginning of the reign of Ahaz; and was fulfilled by Tiglath-pileser's taking Damascus, and carrying the people captives to Kir, (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Kgs 16:9</reference>), and overrunning great part of the kingdom of Israel, and carrying a great number of the Israelites also captives to Assyria; and still more fully in regard to Israel, by the conquest of the kingdom, and the captivity of the people, effected a few years after by Shalmaneser. - L. <div eID="gen27223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27224" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27225" type="x-p"/> The burden of Damascus - Which is, according to the common version, The cities of Aroer are forsaken. It has already been observed by the learned prelate that the prophecy, as it relates to Damascus, was executed in the beginning of the reign of Ahaz, probably about the third year. If we credit Midrash, the Damascenes were the most extensive and flagrant of all idolaters. "There were in Damascus three hundred and sixty-five streets, in each of these was an idol, and each idol had his peculiar day of worship; so that the whole were worshipped in the course of the year." This, or any thing like this, was a sufficient reason for this city's destruction. <div eID="gen27225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27226" type="x-p"/> A ruinous heap - For מעי mei, "a ruinous heap," the Septuagint reads לעי lei, "for a ruin," the Vulgate כעי kei, "as a ruin." I follow the former.
entries.952162a4903d63f51a7c2a7a2dd34c599b48dd8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27227" type="x-p"/> The cities of Aroer are forsaken "The cities are deserted for ever" - What has Aroer on the river Arnon to do with Damascus? and if there be another Aroer on the northern border of the tribe of Gad, as Reland seems to think there might be, this is not much more to the purpose. Besides, the cities of Aroer, if Aroer itself is a city, makes no good sense. The Septuagint, for ערער aroer, read עדי עד adey ad, εις τον αιωνα, for ever, or for a long duration. The Chaldee takes the word for a verb from ערה arah, translating it חרבו cherebu, devastabuntur, "they shall be wasted." The Syriac read עדועיר adoeir. So that the reading is very doubtful. I follow the Septuagint as making the plainest sense.
entries.d7f5c85fba9a932c511b195fddd81725db07935a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27228" type="x-p"/> The remnant of Syria "The pride of Syria" - For שאר shear, "remnant," Houbigant reads שאת seeth, "pride," answering, as the sentence seems evidently to require, to כבוד cabod, "the glory of Israel." The conjecture is so very probable that I venture to follow it. <div eID="gen27228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27229" type="x-p"/> As the glory - בכבוד bichbod, "In the glory," is the reading of eight MSS., and ten editions.
entries.753607ef578fdb0f5b3666ed14369edb378d6328: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27230" type="x-p"/> In that day - That is, says Kimchi, the time when the ten tribes of Israel, which were the glory of Jacob, should be carried into captivity.
entries.b517c014ca2774dfd4f47d2e4ce9cc9853b5a9df: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27231" type="x-p"/> As when the harvestman gathereth "As when one gathereth" - That is, the king of Assyria shall sweep away the whole body of the people, as the reaper strippeth off the whole crop of corn; and the remnant shall be no more in proportion than the scattered ears left to the gleaner. The valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem was celebrated for its plentiful harvest; it is here used poetically for any fruitful country. One MS., and one ancient edition, has באסף beesoph, "In gathering," instead of כאסף keesoph, "AS the gathering."
entries.3fa08b5eaaa4be81fbd5c2cf1621013890b1e04d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27232" type="x-p"/> The altars, the work of his hands "The altars dedicated to the work of his hands" - The construction of the words, and the meaning of the sentence, in this place are not obvious; all the ancient Versions, and most of the modern, have mistaken it. The word מעשה maaseh, "the work," stands in regimine with מזבחות mizbechoth, "altars," not in opposition to it; it means the, altars of the work of their hand; that is of the idols, which are the work of their hands. Thus Kimchi has explained it, and Le Clerc has followed him.
entries.f6ce9a7b41b02885c297bfe507b33a9793b50b71: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27233" type="x-p"/> As a forsaken bough, and an uppermost branch "the Hivites and the Amorites" - החרש והאמיר hachoresh vehaamir. No one has ever yet been able to make any tolerable sense of these words. The translation of the Septuagint has happily preserved what seems to be the true reading of the text, as it stood in the copies of their time; though the words are now transposed, either in the text or in their Version; οἱ Αμαρῥαιοι και οἱ Ευαιοι, "the Amorites and the Hivites." It is remarkable that many commentators, who never thought of admitting the reading of the Septuagint, understand the passage as referring to that very event which their Version expresses; so that it is plain that nothing can be more suitable to the context. "My father," says Bishop Lowth, "saw the necessity of admitting this variation at a time when it was not usual to make so free with the Hebrew text." Mr. Parkhurst is not satisfied with the prelate's adoption of the reading of the Septuagint, "the Hivites and the Amorites." He thinks the difficult words should be thus rendered; he takes the whole verse: "And his fortified cities shall be like the leaving, or what is left כעזובת caazubath, of or in a ploughed field, החרש hachoresh, or on a branch which they leave coram, before, the children of Israel." Which he considers a plain reference to the Mosaic laws relative to the not gleaning of their ploughed fields, vineyards, and oliveyards, but leaving עזב ozeb, somewhat of the fruits, for the poor of the land; <reference osisRef="Lev.9.9">Lev 9:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.9.10">Lev 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.24.19-Deu.24.21">Deu 24:19-21</reference>, in the Hebrew. I fear that the text is taken by storm on both interpretations. One MS. has כל ערי col arey, "all the cities;" and instead of החלש hachalash, "of the branch," six MSS. have החדש hachodesh, "of the month." But this is probably a mistake.
entries.0a450d918cc60b3077a1364164f6f3ab9331bce1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27234" type="x-p"/> Strange slips "Shoots from a foreign soil" - The pleasant plants, and shoots from a foreign soil, are allegorical expressions for strange and idolatrous worship; vicious and abominable practices connected with it; reliance on human aid, and on alliances entered into with the neighboring nations, especially Egypt; to all which the Israelites were greatly addicted, and in their expectations from which they should be grievously disappointed.
entries.a0a296c4867421829ed3537199c56fc84eb02491: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27235" type="x-p"/> Wo to the multitude - The three last verses of this chapter seem to have no relation to the foregoing prophecy, to which they are joined. It is a beautiful piece, standing singly and by itself; for neither has it any connection with what follows: whether it stands in its right place, or not, I cannot say. It is a noble description of the formidable invasion and the sudden overthrow of Sennacherib; which is intimated in the strongest terms and the most expressive images, exactly suitable to the event. <div eID="gen27235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27236" type="x-p"/> Like the rushing of mighty waters! - Five words, three at the end of the twelfth verse, and two at the beginning of the thirteenth, are omitted in eight MSS., with the Syriac; that is, in effect, the repetition contained in the first line of <reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">Isa 17:13</reference> in this translation, is not made. After having observed that it is equally easy to account for the omission of these words by a transcriber if they are genuine, or their insertion if they are not genuine, occasioned by his carrying his eye backwards to the word לאמים leammim, or forwards to ישאון yeshaon, I shall leave it to the reader's judgment to determine whether they are genuine or not. Instead of כהמות cahamoth, "as the roaring," five MSS. and the Vulgate have כהמון kehamon, "as the multitude."
entries.3cbe041137245897533163e3373628d453e0b4b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27237" type="x-p"/> He is not "He is no more" - For איננו einennu ten MSS. of Dr. Kennicott's, (three ancient), ten of De Rossi's, and two editions, and the Septuagint, Syriac, Chaldee, Vulgate, and Arabic, have ואיננו veeinenno. This particle, authenticated by so many good vouchers, restores the sentence to its true poetical form, implying a repetition of some part of the parallel line preceding, thus: - "At the season of evening, behold terror! <div eID="gen27237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27238" type="x-p"/> Before the morning, and [behold] he is no more!" <div eID="gen27238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27239" type="x-p"/> That spoil us - For שוסינו shoseynu, them that spoil us, fifteen MSS., one edition, and the Syriac have שוסנו shosenu, him that spoileth us. And for לבזזינו lebozezeynu, them that rob us, six MSS. and the Syriac have לבוזזנו lebozzeno, him that robbeth us: and these readings make the place answer better to Sennacherib, according to Lowth's conjecture. Though God may permit the wicked to prevail for a time against his people, yet in the end those shall be overthrown, and the glory of the Lord shall shine brightly on them that fear him; for the earth shall be subdued, and the universe filled with his glory. Amen, and Amen!  <chapter eID="Isa.17"/> <div eID="gen27239" type="x-p"/>

entries.16887fa3843bea5ee4ab440b1516d47bc369e523: <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1-Isa.17.3">Isa 17:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13031" type="x-p"/> The first turn: <hi type="italic">“Behold, Damascus must </hi>(<hi type="italic">be taken</hi>)<hi type="italic">away out of the number of the cities, and will be a heap of fallen ruins. The cities of Aroer are forsaken, they are given up to flocks, they lie there without any one scaring them away. And the fortress of Ephraim is abolished, and the kingdom of Damascus; and it happens to those that are left of Aram as to the glory of the sons of Israel, saith Jehovah of hosts.”</hi> “<hi type="italic">Behold</hi>,” etc.: <hi type="italic">hinnēh</hi> followed by a participle indicates here, as it does everywhere else, something very near at hand. Damascus is removed מעיר (= עיר מהיות, cf., 1Ki 15:13), i.e., out of the sphere of existence as a city. It becomes מעי, a heap of ruins. The word is used intentionally instead of עי, to sound as much as possible like מעיר: a mutilated city, so to speak. It is just the same with Israel, which has made itself an appendage of Damascus. The “cities of Aroer” (<hi type="italic">gen. appos.</hi> Ges. §114, 3) represent the land to the east of the Jordan: there the judgment upon Israel (executed by Tiglath-pileser) first began. There were two <hi type="italic">Aroers</hi>: an old Amoritish city allotted to the tribe of Reuben, viz., “Aroer on the Arnon” (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.36">Deu 2:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.12">Deu 3:12</reference>, etc.); and an old Ammonitish one, allotted to the tribe of Gad, viz., “Aroer before Rabbah” (Rabbath, Ammon, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.25">Jos 13:25</reference>). The ruins of the former are <hi type="italic">Arair</hi>, on the lofty northern bank of the <hi type="italic">Mugib</hi>; but the situation of the latter has not yet been determined with certainty (see Comm. on <reference osisRef="Josh.13.25">Jos 13:25</reference>). The “cities of Aroer” are these two Aroers, and the rest of the cities similar to it on the east of the Jordan; just as “the Orions” in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Isa 13:10</reference> are Orion and other similar stars. We meet here again with a significant play upon the sound in the expression <hi type="italic">‛ârē</hi> <hi type="italic">‛Aro‛ēr</hi> (cities of Aroer): the name of Aroer was ominous, and what its name indicated would happen to the cities in its circuit. ערער means “to lay bare,” to pull down (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.58">Jer 51:58</reference>); and ערער, ערירי signifies a stark-naked condition, a state of desolation and solitude. After <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference> has threatened Damascus in particular, and <reference osisRef="Isa.17.2">Isa 17:2</reference> has done the same to Israel, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.3">Isa 17:3</reference> comprehends them both. Ephraim loses the fortified cities which once served it as defences, and Damascus loses its rank as a kingdom. Those that are left of Aram, who do not fall in the war, become like the proud citizens of the kingdom of Israel, i.e., they are carried away into captivity. All this was fulfilled under Tiglath-pileser. The accentuation connects ארם שׁאר (the remnant of Aram) with the first half of the verse; but the meaning remains the same, as the subject to יהיוּ is in any case the Aramaeans.
entries.e95deaa02daec6d1509d78f4c1ca25c5749a0fab: <reference osisRef="Isa.17.4-Isa.17.8">Isa 17:4-8</reference> <div eID="gen13031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13032" type="x-p"/> Second turn: <hi type="italic">“And it comes to pass in that day, the glory of Jacob wastes away, and the fat of his flesh grows thin. And it will be as when a reaper grasps the stalks of wheat, and his arm mows off the ears; and it will be as with one who gathers together ears in the valley of Rephaim. Yet a gleaning remains from it, as at the olive-beating: two, three berries high up at the top; four, five in its, the fruit tree’s, branches, saith Jehovah the God of Israel. At that day will man look up to his Creator, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel. And he will not look to the altars, the work of his hands; and what his fingers have made he will not regard, neither the Astartes nor the sun-gods.”</hi> This second turn does not speak of Damascus, but simply of Israel, and in fact of all Israel, the range of vision widening out from Israel in the more restricted sense, so as to embrace the whole. It will all disappear, with the exception of a small remnant; but the latter will return. Thus “a remnant will return,” the law of Israel’s history, which is here shown first of all in its threatening aspect, and then in its more promising one. The reputation and prosperity to which the two kingdoms were raised by Jeroboam II and Uzziah would pass away. Israel was ripe for judgment, like a field of corn for the harvest; and it would be as when a reaper grasps the stalks that have shot up, and cuts off the ears. קציר is not used elliptically for קציר אישׁ (Gesenius), nor is it a definition of time (Luzzatto), nor an accusative of the object (Knobel), but a noun formed like נביא, פליל, פריץ, and used in the sense of reaper (<hi type="italic">kōtzēr</hi> in other cases).<note placement="foot">Instead of <hi type="italic">kâtzar</hi> (to cut off, or shorten), they now say <hi type="italic">kâratz</hi> in the whole of the land to the east of the Jordan, which gives the idea of sawing off - a much more suitable one where the Syrian sickle is used.</note> <div eID="gen13032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13033" type="x-p"/> The figure suggested here is more fully expanded in John 4 and Rev 14. Hardly a single one will escape the judgment: just as in the broad plain of Rephaim, which slopes off to the south-west of Jerusalem as far as Bethlehem, where it is covered with rich fields of wheat, the collectors of ears leave only one or two ears lying scattered here and there. <div eID="gen13033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13034" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless a gleaning of Israel (“in it,” viz., in Jacob, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.4">Isa 17:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference>) will be left, just as when the branches of the olive tree, which have been already cleared with the hand, are still further shaken with a stick, there still remain a few olives upon the highest branch (two, three; cf., 2Ki 9:32), or concealed under the foliage of the branches. “<hi type="italic">Its</hi>, <hi type="italic">the fruit tree's</hi>, <hi type="italic">branches</hi>:” this is an elegant expression, as, for example, in <reference osisRef="Prov.14.13">Pro 14:13</reference>; the carrying over of the ה to the second word is very natural in both passages (see Ges. §121,<hi type="italic">b</hi>). This small remnant will turn with stedfast gaze to the living God, as is becoming in man as such (<hi type="italic">hâ'âdâm</hi>), and not regard the idols as worthy of any look at all, at least of any reverential look. As <hi type="italic">hammânim</hi> are here images of the sun-god חמן בעל, which is well known from the Phoenician monuments,<note placement="foot">See Levy, <hi type="italic">Phönizisches Wörterbuch</hi> (1864), p. 19; and Otto Strauss on <hi type="italic">Nahum</hi>, p. xxii. ss.</note><hi type="italic">'ashērim</hi> (for which we find, though more rarely, <hi type="italic">'ashēroth</hi>) apparently signifies images of the moon-goddess. And the combination of “Baal, Asherah, and all the host of heaven” in 2Ki 23:4, as well as the surname “queen of heaven” in <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">Jer 7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.18-Jer.44.19">Jer 44:18-19</reference>, appears to require this (Knobel). But the latest researches have proved that <hi type="italic">'Ashērâh</hi> is rather the Semitic Aphrodite, and therefore the planet Venus, which was called the “little luck” (<hi type="italic">es</hi>-<hi type="italic">sa‛d el</hi>-<hi type="italic">as'gar</hi>)<note placement="foot">See Krehl, <hi type="italic">Religion der vorislamischen Araber</hi> (1863), p. 11.</note> by the Arabs, in distinction from <hi type="italic">Musteri</hi> (Jupiter),<note placement="foot">This was the <hi type="italic">tutelar</hi> deity of Damascus; see <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, Appendix.</note> or “the great luck.” And with this the name <hi type="italic">'Asherah</hi> the “lucky” (i.e., the source of luck or prosperity) and the similar surname given to the Assyrian <hi type="italic">Istar</hi> agree;<note placement="foot">“<hi type="italic">Ishtar</hi>,” says Rawlinson in his <hi type="italic">Five Great Monarchies of the Ancient Eastern World</hi>, - a work which challenges criticism through its dazzling results - ”<hi type="italic">Ishtar</hi> is the goddess who rejoices mankind, and her most common epithet is Amra, 'the fortunate' or 'the happy.' But otherwise her epithets are vague and general, insomuch that she is often scarcely distinguishable from Beltis (the wife of Bel-Nimrod).” Vid., vol. i. p. 175 (1862).</note> for <hi type="italic">'Asherah</hi> is the very same goddess as <hi type="italic">'Ashtoreth</hi>, whose name is thoroughly Arian, and apparently signifies the star (Ved. <hi type="italic">stir</hi> = <hi type="italic">star</hi>; Zend. <hi type="italic">stare</hi>; Neo-Pers. <hi type="italic">sitâre</hi>, used chiefly for the morning star), although Rawlinson (without being able to suggest any more acceptable interpretation) speaks of this view as “not worthy of much attention.”<note placement="foot">The planet Venus, according to a Midrash relating to <reference osisRef="Gen.6.1-Gen.6.2">Gen 6:1-2</reference>, is <hi type="italic">'Istehar</hi> transferred to the sky; and this is the same as <hi type="italic">Zuhare</hi> (see Geiger, <hi type="italic">Was hat Muhammed</hi>, etc. 1833, pp. 107-109).</note> <div eID="gen13034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13035" type="x-p"/> Thus <hi type="italic">Asherim</hi> is used to signify the <hi type="italic">bosquets</hi> (shrubberies) or trees dedicated to the Semitic Aphrodite (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.21">Deu 16:21</reference>; compare the verbs used to signify their removal, גדע, כרת, נתשׁ); but here it probably refers to her statues or images<note placement="foot">The plural <hi type="italic">Ashtaroth</hi>, <hi type="italic">Hathors</hi>, which occurs upon Assyrian and Egyptian monuments, has a different meaning.</note> (2Ki 21:7; compare the <hi type="italic">miphletzeth</hi> in 1Ki 15:13, which is used to denote an obscene exhibition). For these images of the sun-god and of the goddess of the morning star, the remnant of Israel, that has been purified by the smelting furnace of judgment, has no longer any eye. Its looks are exclusively directed to the one true God of man. The promise, which here begins to dawn at the close of the second turn, is hidden again in the third, though only to break forth again in the fourth with double or triple intensity.
entries.6bfb7dc80f2783f56b6ab55ac1c67df5d9ed5f75: <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9-Isa.17.11">Isa 17:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen13035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13036" type="x-p"/> Third turn: <hi type="italic">“In that day will his fortified cities be like the ruins of the forest and of the mountain top, which they cleared before the sons of Israel: and there arises a waste place. For thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation, and hast not thought of the Rock of thy stronghold, therefore thou plantedst charming plantations, and didst set them with strange vines. In the day that thou plantedst, thou didst make a fence; and with the morning dawn thou madest thy sowing to blossom: a harvest heap in the day of deep wounds and deadly sorrow of heart.”</hi> The statement in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.3">Isa 17:3</reference>, “The fortress of Ephraim is abolished,” is repeated in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9">Isa 17:9</reference> in a more descriptive manner. The fate of the strongly fortified cities of Ephraim would be the same as that of the old Canaanitish castles, which were still to be discerned in their antiquated remains, either in the depths of forests or high up on the mountains. The word <hi type="italic">‛azubâh</hi>, which the early translators quite misunderstood, signifies, both here and in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.12">Isa 6:12</reference>, desolate places that have gone to ruin. They also misunderstood והאמיר הסהרשׁ. The Septuagint renders it, by a bold conjecture, οἱ Αμοῤῥηαῖοι καὶ οὶ Εὐαῖοι; but this is at once proved to be false by the inversion of the names of the two peoples, which was very properly thought to be necessary. האמיר undoubtedly signifies the top of a tree, which is quite unsuitable here. But as even this meaning points back to אמר, <hi type="italic">extollere</hi>, <hi type="italic">efferre</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.94.4">Psa 94:4</reference>), it may also mean the mountain-top. The name <hi type="italic">hâ'emori</hi> (the Amorites: those who dwell high up in the mountains) proves the possibility of this; and the prophet had this name in his mind, and was guided by it in his choice of a word. The subject of עזבוּ is self-evident. And the reason why only the ruins in forests and on mountains are mentioned is, that other places, which were situated on the different lines of traffic, merely changed their inhabitants when the land was taken by Israel. The reason why the fate of Ephraim’s fortified castles was the same as that of the Amoritish castles, which were then lying in ruins, was that Ephraim, as stated in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.10">Isa 17:10</reference>, had turned away from its true rocky stronghold, namely from Jehovah. It was a consequence of this estrangement from God, that Ephraim planted נעמנים נטעי, plantations of the nature of pleasant things, or pleasant plantations (compare on <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49">Psa 78:49</reference>, and Ewald, §287, <hi type="italic">ab</hi>), i.e., cultivated all kinds of sensual accompaniments to its worship, in accordance with its heathen propensities; and sowed, or rather (as <hi type="italic">zemōrâh</hi> is the layer of a vine) “set,” this garden-ground, to which the suffix <hi type="italic">ennu</hi> refers, with strange grapes, by forming an alliance with a <hi type="italic">zâr</hi> (a stranger), namely the king of Damascus. On the very day of the planting, Ephraim fenced it carefully (this is the meaning of the <hi type="italic">pilpel</hi>, <hi type="italic">sigsēg</hi> from שׂוּג = סוּג, not “to raise,” as no such verb as שׂוּג = שׂגה, סגא, can be shown to exist), that is to say, he ensured the perpetuity of these sensuous modes of worship as a state religion, with all the shrewdness of a Jeroboam (see <reference osisRef="Amos.7.13">Amo 7:13</reference>). And the very next morning he had brought into blossom what he had sown: the foreign layer had shot up like a hot-house plant, i.e., the alliance had speedily grown into a hearty agreement, and had already produced one blossom at any rate, viz., the plan of a joint attack upon Judah. But this plantation, which was so flattering and promising for Israel, and which had succeeded so rapidly, and to all appearance so happily, was a harvest heap for the day of the judgment. Nearly all modern expositors have taken <hi type="italic">nēd</hi> as the third person (after the form <hi type="italic">mēth</hi>, Ges. §72, Anm. 1), and render it “the harvest flees;” but the third person of נוּד would be נד, like the participle in <reference osisRef="Gen.4.12">Gen 4:12</reference>; whereas the meaning <hi type="italic">cumulus</hi> (a heap), which it has elsewhere as a substantive, is quite appropriate, and the statement of the prophet resembles that of the apostle in Rom 2:5. The day of the judgment is called “the day of נחלה” (or, according to another reading, נחלה), not, however, as equivalent to <hi type="italic">nachal</hi>, a stream (Luzzatto, <hi type="italic">in giorno di fiumana</hi>), as in <reference osisRef="Ps.124.4">Psa 124:4</reference> (the tone upon the last syllable proves this), nor in the sense of “in the day of possession,” as Rosenmüller and others suppose, since this necessarily gives to נד the former objectionable and (by the side of קציר) improbable verbal sense; but as the feminine of <hi type="italic">nachleh</hi>, written briefly for <hi type="italic">maccâh</hi> <hi type="italic">nachlâh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.17">Jer 14:17</reference>), i.e., inasmuch as it inflicts grievous and mortal wounds. Ephraim’s plantation is a harvest heap for that day (compare <hi type="italic">kâtzir</hi>, the harvest of punishment, in Hos 6:11 and <reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">Jer 51:33</reference>); and the hope set upon this plantation is changed into אנוּשׁ כּאב, a desperate and incurable heartfelt sorrow (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.15">Jer 30:15</reference>). The organic connection between <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.14">Isa 17:12-14</reference>, which follow, and the oracle concerning Damascus and Israel, has also been either entirely misunderstood, or not thoroughly appreciated. The connection is the following: As the prophet sets before himself the manner in which the sin of Ephraim is punished by Asshur, as the latter sweeps over the Holy Land, the promise which already began to dawn in the second turn bursts completely through: the world-power is the instrument of punishment in the hands of Jehovah, but not for ever.
entries.d70aea05a22b8af388aebb6f128767fe76c3c605: <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.14">Isa 17:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen13036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13037" type="x-p"/> Fourth turn: <hi type="italic">“Woe to the raoring of many nations: like the roaring of seas they roar; and to the rumbling of nations, like the rumbling of mighty waters they rumble! Nations, like the rumbling of many waters they rumble; and He threatens it: then it flies far away, and is chased like chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a cloud of dust before the gale. At eventide, behold consternation; and before the morning dawn it is destroyed: this the portion of our plunderers, and the lot of our robbers.”</hi> It is the destruction of Asshur that the prophet is predicting here (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.24-Isa.14.27">Isa 14:24-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5-Isa.29.8">Isa 29:5-8</reference>, etc.), though not of Asshur as Asshur, but of Asshur as the imperial kingdom, which embraced a multitude of nations (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Isa 22:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa 8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.10">Isa 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.26">Isa 14:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">Isa 29:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.8">Isa 29:8</reference>) all gathered together under the rule of one will, to make a common attack upon the church of God. The connection between this fourth turn and the third is precisely the same as between <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa 8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.10">Isa 8:10</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Isa 8:6</reference>-8. The exclamation of woe (<hi type="italic">hoi</hi>) is an expression of pain, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1">Isa 10:1</reference>; and this is followed by a proclamation of the judgment of wrath. The description of the rolling wave of nations is as pictorial as the well-known <hi type="italic">illi inter sese</hi>, etc., of the Cyclops in Virgil. “It spreads and stretches out, as if it would never cease to roll, and roar, and surge, and sweep onward in its course” (Drechsler). In the expression “it” (<hi type="italic">bo</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">Isa 17:13</reference>, the many surging nations are kneaded together, as it were, into one mass. It costs God simply a threatening word; and this mass all flies apart (<hi type="italic">mimmerchâk</hi> like <hi type="italic">mērâchōk</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.7">Isa 23:7</reference>), and falls into dust, and whirls about in all directions, like the chaff of threshing-floors in high situations, or like dust whirled up by the storm. The judgment commences in the evening, and rages through the night; and before the morning dawns, the army of nations raised by the imperial power is all destroyed (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">Isa 29:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.8">Isa 29:8</reference>, and the fulfilment in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference>). The fact that the oracle concerning Damascus in its fourth stage takes so comprehensive and, so far as Israel is concerned, so promising a form, may be explained on the ground that Syria was the forerunner of Asshur in the attack upon Israel, and that the alliance between Israel and Syria became the occasion of the complications with Asshur. If the substance of the <hi type="italic">massâ Dammesek</hi> (the oracle concerning Damascus) had been restricted to the prophecy contained in the name Mahershalal, the element of promise so characteristic of the prophecies against the nations of the world would be entirely wanting. But the shout of triumph, “This is the portion,” etc., supplied a terminal point, beyond which the <hi type="italic">massa</hi> could not go without the sacrifice of its unity. We are therefore warranted in regarding <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference> as an independent prophecy, notwithstanding its commencement, which apparently forms a continuation of the fourth strophe of <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>-14. Ethiopia’s Submission to Jehovah - <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference> <div eID="gen13037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13038" type="x-p"/> The notion that <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4-Isa.18.6">Isa 18:4-6</reference> contains an account of the judgment of Jehovah upon Ethiopia is quite an untenable one. The prophet is here predicting the destruction of the army of Sennacherib in his usual way, and in accordance with the actual fulfilment (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference>). The view which Hofmann has adopted from the Jewish expositors - namely, that the people so strangely described at the commencement and close of the prophecy is the Israelitish nation - is equally untenable. It is Ethiopia. Taking both these facts together, then, the conclusion to which we are brought is, that the prophet is here foretelling the effect that will be produced upon Ethiopia by the judgment which Jehovah is about to inflict upon Asshur. But it is altogether improbable either that the prophecy falls later than the Assyrian expedition against Egypt (as Schegg supposes), or that the Ethiopian ambassadors mentioned here are despatched to Judah to seek for friendship and aid (as Ewald, Knobel, Meier, and Thenius maintain). The expedition was still impending, and that against Judah was the means to this further end. The ambassadors are not sent to Judah, but carry commands with the most stirring despatch to every province under Ethiopian rule. The Ethiopian kingdom is thrown into the greatest excitement in the face of the approaching Assyrian invasion, and the messengers are sent out to raise the militia. At that time both Egypts were governed by the Ethiopian (or twenty-fifth) dynasty, <hi type="italic">Sabako</hi> the Ethiopian having made himself master of the country on the Lower Nile.<note placement="foot">See Brugsch, <hi type="italic">Histoire d'Egypte</hi>, i. (1859) 244-246.</note> <div eID="gen13038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13039" type="x-p"/> The king of Egypt who was contemporaneous with Sennacherib was the <hi type="italic">Tirhaka</hi> of the Old Testament, the <hi type="italic">Tarakos</hi> of Manetho, and the <hi type="italic">Tearkon</hi> of Strabo - a great conqueror, according to Megasthenes, like Sesostris and Nebuchadnezzar, who had carried his conquests as far as the Pillars of Hercules (Strabo, xv 1, 6). This explains the strangely sounding description given in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference> of the Ethiopian people, which had the universal reputation in antiquity of gigantic strength and invincibility. It is impossible to determine the length of time that intervened between the composition of the prophecy and the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, in which the Assyrian army commenced the expedition across Judah to Egypt. The event which the prophecy foretells - namely, that the judgment of Jehovah upon Asshur would be followed by the submission of Ethiopia to Jehovah - was only partially and provisionally fulfilled (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.23">2Ch 32:23</reference>). And there is nothing to surprise us in this, inasmuch as in the prophecies delivered before the destruction of Assyria the latter always presented itself to the mind of the prophet as the kingdom of the world; and consequently the prophecy had also an eschatological feature, which still remained for a future and remote fulfilment.  <chapter eID="Isa.17"/> <div eID="gen13039" type="x-p"/>

entries.5f692734df8091c3a740338e301da621ee40b0b8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.17.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.17.1" sID="gen43199" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi><hi type="italic"> The burden of Damascus.</hi> Here he prophesies against the kingdom of Syria, and mentions the chief city in which the seat of the kingdom lay. It was proper that this calamity, like others which came before it, should be described, that the righteous might confidently believe that God would one day assist them, and would not always permit them to be oppressed by the wicked without end. The king of Syria had formed an alliance with Israel against Judah, as we saw formerly in the seventh chapter; and as the Jews were not able to contend with him, and were deprived of other aids, they might also entertain doubts about God’s assistance, as if he had utterly abandoned them. To free them, therefore, from these doubts, he threatens the destruction of that kingdom, from which they would readily conclude that God fought in defense of his people.<div eID="gen43200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43201" type="x-p"/>It is uncertain at what time Isaiah uttered this prophecy, for, as I have already remarked, he does not follow the order of time in threatening against each nation the punishment which it deserved. But, as far as I am able to conjecture, he foretold those events at the time when those two kings, that is, the kings of Israel and Syria, invaded Judea, and entered into a league to destroy it and the whole Church, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.1 Bible:Isa.7.2">Isaiah 7:1, 2</reference>;) for, by joining together the Israelites and the Syrians, he summons them to a mutual judgment, in order to show that the only advantage which they had derived from the wicked and disgraceful conspiracy was, to be involved in the same destruction. In this manner Isaiah intended to comfort godly persons who were of the tribe of Judah; for he has his eye chiefly on them, that they may not be discouraged, and not on the Syrians, or even the Israelites, whose destruction he foretells.<div eID="gen43201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43202" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Behold, Damascus is taken away.</hi> The demonstrative particle, <hi type="italic">Behold,</hi> seals the certainty of the prophecy. When he expressly mentions <hi type="italic">Damascus,</hi> it does not follow from this that the other parts of the kingdom are exempted, but it was customary with the prophets to take a part for the whole, so as to include under the destruction of the metropolis the fate of the whole nation; for what must ordinary towns expect when the citadel of the kingdom has been stormed? Yet there is another reason why the Prophets pronounce heavier threatenings on the chief and royal cities, and especially direct their discourse against them. It is, because a polluted flood of crimes overflows from them into the whole country.<div eID="gen43202" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.17.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43199" osisID="Isa.17.1" type="section"/>
entries.dc29732a95c2dc02e78bf5aafb0c97e0ff4bb149: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.17.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.17.2" sID="gen43203" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">The cities of Aroer are forsaken.</hi> It is not probable that <hi type="italic">Aroer</hi> here denotes the city which is mentioned elsewhere, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Num.32.34 Bible:Deut.2.36 Bible:Deut.3.12 Bible:Deut.4.48">Numbers 32:34; Deuteronomy 2:36, 3:12, 4:48</reference>;) but it is rather the name of a country. He draws the picture of a country which has been ruined; for he shews that those places in which cities had been built will be devoted to pasture, and that no habitation will be left there but huts and shepherds’ tents; for if any inhabitants remained, the shepherds would drive their flocks to some other place.<div eID="gen43204" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.17.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43203" osisID="Isa.17.2" type="section"/>
entries.9859368b0f23c3790a8b1d31b7f9daa54c557439: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.17.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.17.3" sID="gen43205" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43206" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">The fortress shall cease.</hi> <note n="4"> <div sID="gen43207" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Le secours venant d’Ephraim cessara</foreign>;” — “The assistance coming from Ephraim shall cease.”<div eID="gen43207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43208" type="x-p"/> FT262 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sera diminué</foreign>;” — “Shall be made thin.” — Eng.
